TextView.android:text: Advanced Lesson 19: Complex Numbers in Geometry

In geometry, we can represent every point (x, y) in the plane as a single complex number z = x + iy. This simple shift allows us to use algebraic operations for geometric transformations. Adding a complex number simply translates a point. Multiplying by a complex number r*e^(it) performs a rotation by angle t and a scaling by factor r. This makes finding images of shapes under rotation or scaling trivially easy.

The expression (a-b)/(c-b) is a complex number whose argument is the angle between lines AB and CB. If this value is purely imaginary, the lines are perpendicular! This is one of the most powerful tricks in the Olympiad toolbox. When we need to prove that lines meet at 90 degrees, we don't need to measure angles. We just check if the ratio of their differences is purely imaginary. It turns complex geometric proofs into simple complex multiplication.

Many classical geometry theorems, like those concerning concurrency and collinearity, become almost trivial with complex numbers. By representing points as complex numbers z1, z2, z3, we can derive ratios and proportions using simple algebraic identities. This avoids the clutter of classical Euclidean proofs and allows for systematic, fast, and rigorous solutions, even for the most intimidating geometry problems.
Prove that the lines connecting the vertices of a triangle to the contact points of the incircle are concurrent.

Solution: This is Gergonne's Theorem. Let the contact points of the incircle on sides BC, CA, AB be X, Y, Z. Let a, b, c be the side lengths. The contact points X, Y, Z in barycentric or complex coordinate representation depend only on the distances from vertices to the tangency points. Specifically, the vectors to X, Y, Z can be represented as (s-a), (s-b), (s-c). Using the complex form of Ceva's Theorem, we check if the product of the ratios (AX/XB) * (BY/YC) * (CZ/ZA) equals 1. By calculating these ratios using the complex coordinates of the points X, Y, Z, all terms cancel perfectly. Since the product is 1, the lines are concurrent. Proof complete.
